verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents, of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant [is] the dwelling of brothers also together.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing, a song of David. Look, only look: how good it is, and how sweet, when brothers sit down together and stay.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open with the pilgrim's breath. This is one of the fifteen Songs of the Ascents (Psalms 120–134), sung by those going up to Jerusalem for the three festivals, and the title says 'ascents' (maʿalot), literally 'steps'. The KJV's 'degrees' is the Latin gradus, 'steps', which means nothing to a modern ear. Play it as a crowd, not a soloist: people on a road, tired, finally in sight of the city, turning to each other.

The word hinneh, 'behold', is an instruction to look, as if the thing is in front of you. The KJV 'how good and how pleasant it is' adds an 'it is' that the Hebrew lacks; the two exclamations 'mah tov umah naʿim' stand bare, as a gasp. The key word is shevet, 'dwelling', literally 'sitting/staying'. This is not a feeling of harmony but the concrete fact of brothers living under one roof or on one inheritance, which in the ancient Near East is exactly where brothers tended to fall out, over land, flocks and the father's estate. The KJV 'in unity' makes it a moral quality; the Hebrew 'gam yachad', 'also together', is a plain, almost surprised observation. Ibn Ezra notes that 'good and pleasant' are adjectives with the noun omitted ('what a good thing'), which is why the line feels so spare.

Traditional readers heard more: Rashi takes 'brothers' as Israel, whom God dwells among in the Temple; Radak as the king and the high priest, brothers in greatness; Metzudat David as the whole house of Israel on its own land and in one kingdom.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive construct of yashav, 'to sit, stay, dwell': the concrete act of settling together, not an abstract concord. It is the same verb used for living on a shared estate.
'Ascents' or 'steps', from the verb 'to go up'. The title marks the psalm as one of the fifteen pilgrim songs; the KJV 'degrees' is a transliteration of Latin gradus.
'Pleasant, sweet'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as a matter of sweetness and agreeableness, a sensory word rather than a moral one.

verses.translation_literal: Like the good oil upon the head, going down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, that goes down upon the mouth of his garments.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is like the good oil poured on the head, heavy and fragrant, running down into the beard, the beard of Aaron, and still running, down to the opening of his robes.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the picture, and it is deliberately excessive. Nobody pours oil so that it runs down the beard and into the collar; the point is abundance, oil that cannot be contained. Aaron's anointing (Exodus 29:7, Leviticus 8:12) used a blend of myrrh, cinnamon, cane and cassia in olive oil (Exodus 30:22–25), costly and strongly scented, so the audience should smell it. Radak notes the ointment was compounded and perfumed, and Rashi that it was the oil of anointing.

The KJV makes several choices to watch. 'Precious ointment' translates 'ha-shemen ha-tov', 'the good oil', and the definite article points to the known anointing oil. 'Ran down' and 'went down' put the participles 'yored', 'coming down', into the past: the Hebrew is present and unfinished, the oil is still flowing, and that is the image. The word to listen to is 'midotav'. The KJV 'skirts' sends the oil to the hem; but 'pi' is 'mouth', and Rashi and Radak read 'the mouth of his garments' as the neck opening of the tunic, where the beard rests. So the oil stops at the collar, and the beard is the bridge. The BBE 'face' for 'beard' loses the physical object altogether. The word 'midot' itself usually means 'measures'; here it is clothing (compare 'maddo bad', the linen garment of Leviticus 6:3), as Radak and Metzudat Zion say.

Status: the beard was a mark of adult male dignity, and the priest was the one Israelite whose head was publicly marked with the sacred oil. Rashi also recalls the rabbinic reading of 'brothers' as Moses and Aaron.

philological_notes.note: 'His garments' (literally 'his measures', then the garment cut to fit). Radak and Metzudat Zion gloss it as clothing, like 'maddo bad' in Leviticus 6:3. 'Pi midotav', 'the mouth of his garments', is the neck opening (Rashi, Radak), not the hem.
A participle, 'going down'. Repeated twice: the oil keeps descending, the action does not finish. The KJV turns it into past tense.
'The good' oil. The same word as 'good' in verse 1; the oil is 'good' as the dwelling together is 'good'. The article marks the oil as the known anointing oil (Radak).

verses.translation_literal: Like the dew of Hermon that goes down upon the mountains of Zion; for there YHWH has commanded the blessing: life, unto the age.
verses.translation_dramatic: Like the dew of Hermon, falling soft on the hills of Zion. For there the LORD has spoken the blessing into being: life, for all the ages.
verses.directors_commentary:
A second image, cooler and quieter than the oil. Dew is the summer water of the Land: in the long rainless months between spring and autumn, it is what keeps the crops and the hillsides alive. Mount Hermon, the snow-capped peak on the northern edge of Israel, is the place where dew is heaviest. The audience hears abundance and quiet, the same downward motion as the oil ('yored' again, with the same verb).

The difficulty is geographic: Hermon is some 200 km north of Jerusalem, and its dew does not fall on Zion. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the single 'like' serves two clauses: 'like the dew of Hermon, like the dew that falls on Zion'. The KJV supplies a second 'as the dew' to do that, which the Hebrew does not write. Meiri reads the line differently: the kingship on Zion is as sweet as Hermon's dew in its own place. Do not play it as science; play it as a pilgrim's hyperbole, where the greatest mountain's dew is imagined pouring over the little hills of the city. 'Harrei Tziyyon', 'mountains of Zion', is plural, as Radak notes, like 'Jerusalem, mountains round about her'.

Then the turn: 'ki sham', 'for there'. The reason for the whole psalm is a place. 'Tzivvah', 'commanded', is the verb of royal decree: the KJV's rendering is accurate here, but hear it as an order given, not a wish: the blessing exists because YHWH ordered it. The last two words, 'chayyim ʿad haʿolam', 'life unto the age', are bare, without 'even' (the KJV adds it). The KJV renders YHWH as 'the Lord'; the literal layer keeps the name.

philological_notes.note: 'Dew'. In the Land's rainless summer it is the water on which crops depend, so 'the blessing' here is agricultural as well as spiritual (Ibn Ezra: through dew the grain increases, on which human life depends).
'Commanded': the verb of royal or divine decree. The blessing is not hoped for but ordered; it exists by YHWH's command, and its place is Zion.
'Until the age, forever.' Radak gives two readings: a long time, or the world to come.
